title: 5 things you CANNOT afford to go cheap on for your home gym
summary: NH lists the home gym items worth paying for: barbells, the rack, the platform, machine stations and the training environment itself. He argues quality pays off over ten-plus years and resells well, recommends high-end but not luxury gear, the Rogue Bone Yard, and negotiating mid-range stations through manufacturer salesmen.
claims: Don't buy cheap barbells: an 80-dollar Amazon bar can bend deadlifting 300 lb, has poor knurling and finish, and arrives oil-coated to stop rust
A quality stainless bar needs zero upkeep in any climate; a 300-dollar bar kept 10 years costs 30 dollars a year
Buy high-end but not luxury: beyond a point, as with some boutique bars, you pay double for no meaningful quality gain
Check Rogue's Bone Yard for cosmetically flawed items; he got an Ohio Power Bar for 180 dollars
The rack is your home where you squat, bench, press and do pull-ups; avoid knockoffs that are 40% cheaper but far worse, often with missing pieces and bad service
You need total trust that your safeties will catch any load, and accessory fit depends on rack quality
Garage lifters need a platform: lifting on concrete is hard on feet, ankles and knees and dangerous for drops; build your own with quality materials rather than buying cheap pre-made ones
Quality barbells, racks and stations resell easily at high prices, while cheap knockoff racks won't sell
For stations, contact the manufacturer to get a salesman who can find mid-range options about half the price of gym-grade gear; at home use they still last 10+ years
Brand-name stations like Matrix or Hammer Strength sell like hot cakes, possibly at a profit
His garage gym is cramped and gets very cold and hot, which he tolerates; research and invest in the gym location and environment before buying your first barbell
